newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Political advantage seen from end of Khmer Rouge.
newsitem.headline: Political advantage seen from end of Khmer Rouge.

text.p: The Khmer Rouge guerrilla group looks to be on its last legs but for Cambodia's feuding premiers the end of the Maoist force could hold the key to electoral success, or failure, political analysts said on Sunday.

Khmer Rouge defence chief Son Sen and almost a dozen members of his family were slaughtered in the guerrillas' northern base at Anlong Veng earlier this month. Pol Pot subsequently fled the base but was later captured and arrested by his former comrades.

The surprise break up of the group's top leaders came as First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh and his FUNCINPEC party were negotiating with the rebels in an effort to get them to give up their fight and defect to the government.
Ranariddh says the reason for the talks was peace.
"My only one interest is to bring lasting peace to this country through the end of the Khmer Rouge movement both politically and militarily," the prince told reporters at a party meeting on Friday.
But Ranariddh also said there were electoral gains to be reaped from negotiating an end to the Khmer Rouge and their long war against the government.
"Finally, finally the people of Cambodia will appreciate it through the ballot in 1998," the prince said.

Political analysts said that as well as the glory of ending the war, another potential prize for Ranariddh was an electoral alliance with Khieu Samphan, the Khmer Rouge front man who has long been seen as its acceptable, intellectual face.
Ranariddh and his current uneasy coalition partner, Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, are heading for a close race in a May 23 election, political analysts say.

Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party won a 1993 U.N.-supervised poll with 58 seats in the 120-seat national assembly while Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party (CPP) won 51. Some analysts say next year's election is likely to be closer.

Ranariddh has already formed an alliance with some small parties including the outspoken opposition leader Sam Rainsy. An alliance with Khieu Samphan could secure one or two crucial seats in the provinces, and possibly seal the result for Ranariddh, analysts said.
"In a reasonably free and fair election that might be enough to out-manoeuvre and out-poll the CPP," said Steve Heder, a lecturer at London University's School of Oriental and African Studies.

Khieu Samphan has long been seen as one of Pol Pot's staunchest supporters but for some Cambodians the former teacher and respected member of parliament in the early 1960s retains a lingering respect and reputation for being incorruptible.

"It's the continuing cachet of Khieu Samphan's name," Heder, who is currently in Cambodia, told Reuters. "It has negative associations internationally. It continues to have some positive associations domestically," he said.
"He's had this positive image starting in the late 1950s".
Other analysts agree that Ranariddh's chances in the May election will be improved with Khieu Samphan on his side.
"If there is Khieu Samphan's party, as part of the coalition, it will increase the chance for this electoral coalition," Cambodia expert Raoul Jennar said of Ranariddh's alliance.
But Hun Sen appears determined to prevent his rival from striking any deal with Khieu Samphan.
Earlier this month Hun Sen warned in a speech that the people would attack Khieu Samphan and "hack him with knives" if he ever tried to return to Phnom Penh.

King Norodom Sihanouk said he would only grant an amnesty to Khieu Samphan if both prime ministers agreed but Hun Sen said he would never agree and declared all talks with him and other Khmer Rouge leaders illegal.
Heder said that as well as electoral benefits, Ranariddh stood to gain in other ways from a deal with Khieu Samphan, especially if relations between the two premiers deteriorated further.

"It's putting together a winning electoral coalition. It's also the additional military back-up and a place to hide if it all comes crashing down in Phnom Penh," Heder said, referring to the north Cambodian guerrilla zone.
